analysis.one_liner: Forces drug and device makers to publicly disclose all payments and gifts to doctors.
analysis.headline: The House bill died in committee without a vote, but the identical Senate version became law inside the 2010 health care overhaul, creating a public database of industry payments to doctors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require any company making a drug, device, biological, or medical supply paid for by Medicare, Medicaid, or CHIP to report every payment, gift, honorarium, travel benefit, or ownership stake it gives to a physician worth more than $25, in a yearly electronic filing to the Department of Health and Human Services. Doctors' names, the amounts, the dates, and what the money was for would all be posted on a free, searchable public website so patients could see their own doctor's financial ties to industry. Companies that fail to report would face fines, and the Secretary of Health and Human Services would send yearly summaries to Congress and the states.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients and the public gain a free, searchable record of which doctors took money from which drug and device companies — consulting fees, meals, travel, speaking fees, research funding, and physician ownership stakes. That lets patients judge potential conflicts of interest in their own care, lets journalists and researchers spot patterns, and gives Medicare and Medicaid programs information to police improper influence over prescribing and device choices. Honest physicians also benefit, because the same disclosure rules apply to everyone and public reporting becomes a routine fact of practice rather than a suspicion-raising exception.

how_it_helps.text: Requires drug, device, and medical supply makers paid by Medicare, Medicaid, or CHIP to file annual electronic reports naming every physician who received payments or gifts worth more than $25, the amount, the date, and what it was for — consulting, food, travel, speaking fees, research, and more.

Requires manufacturers, group purchasing organizations, and distributors to disclose any physician or family ownership or investment stake they hold, closing a conflict-of-interest gap that public securities filings do not cover.
Mandates a free, searchable public website — downloadable and aggregated — so any patient can look up what their own doctor received from which company, with a process for doctors to correct errors.
Imposes civil fines from $1,000 up to $1,000,000 for failing to report, and requires the Secretary of Health and Human Services to send annual summary reports to Congress and to the states.

analysis.who_pays: Drug, device, and medical supply manufacturers bear the cost of tracking and reporting every payment above $25 to physicians, and they lose the privacy that previously shielded their marketing and consulting relationships from public view. Physicians with industry ties have those ties exposed on a public website. Group purchasing organizations and distributors must additionally disclose physician ownership interests. The burden is administrative and reputational rather than directly financial for consumers.

drawbacks.text: Payments tied to product research, development, and clinical trials can be hidden from the public database until the product is approved by the FDA or four years pass, so the most commercially significant payments are the last to surface.

Starting in 2010, the bill would preempt state disclosure laws that cover the same payment categories and have different rules, thresholds, or formats, replacing them with one federal standard even where a state law asked for more or faster disclosure.

Penalties are capped at $150,000 per annual filing for ordinary failures to report and $1,000,000 for knowing failures, which is small relative to the marketing budgets of large drug and device companies.
Transfers of $25 or less are excluded, and product samples, short-term device loans, and charity-care items are exempt, leaving some smaller-value industry relationships undisclosed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are real but indirect: patients and researchers could finally see which doctors take industry money and how much, which is the raw material for curbing conflicts of interest in prescribing and device choices. The costs fall mostly on industry in paperwork and public scrutiny, not on consumers. The design concessions — the four-year delay on research payments and preemption of some stricter state rules — tilt the deal toward manufacturers, and the low penalty caps give companies limited financial reason to comply. Overall a modest, well-aimed transparency rule whose main weakness is that disclosure informs but does not itself restrict anything.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees the day it was introduced, never got a hearing or a vote, and expired when the Congress ended — but the same transparency rules were enacted anyway in the 2010 health care law via the Senate bill.

narrative.text: H.R. 3138 was introduced on July 9, 2009 and referred the same day to the House Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means Committees.
On July 10, 2009 it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health, and no further action of any kind was taken for the rest of the 111th Congress.
The bill attracted only one cosponsor in the House.

The parallel Senate version of the Physician Payments Sunshine Act, sponsored by Charles Grassley and Herb Kohl, was incorporated into the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act of 2010, which became law; the government's Open Payments public database of industry payments to physicians launched a few years later.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Patients came out ahead despite the bill dying, because the identical Senate provision became law in the 2010 health care act and a public payments database was built. The industry gave up secrecy about routine payments but kept the four-year reporting delay for research payments.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Patients, via the law that passed anyway

sides.party_line_note: The bill never advanced far enough for a party-line fight — it had one Democratic cosponsor and no recorded votes; the Senate version that became law rode inside the Affordable Care Act, which passed largely along party lines.

industries.note: Companies paid by Medicare, Medicaid, or CHIP would have to file annual reports naming every physician payment over $25 and see them posted on a searchable public website, exposing marketing and consulting spending to patients, journalists, and prosecutors. Their interest in keeping these payments quiet runs against the public's interest in knowing them.

industries.industry: Medical device and medical supply makers
industries.note: Covered device and supply makers face the same reporting duties, including disclosure of physician ownership stakes, and lose the ability to lend or gift products to doctors without a paper trail. Their interest in opaque relationships runs against patient transparency.

Doctors with consulting, speaking, or ownership ties would have those ties listed publicly, with a chance to correct errors. This costs them privacy and reputational control but is the mechanism by which patients learn about their conflicts.

They must report physician ownership and investment interests for the first time, adding compliance work. The bill also carries industry-friendly features — the four-year research-payment reporting delay and preemption of some state rules — that these sectors generally welcomed.
